2. Missingness

miss <- count_missing_values(raw)
tabulate_missing_values(miss)
Missing Values
variable n_missing pct
Parental_Education_Level 90 1.36%
Teacher_Quality 78 1.18%
Distance_from_Home 67 1.01%

3. Imputation

Target (Exam_Score) is complete, so no rows are dropped. The three affected categoricals are mode-imputed.

df <- impute_categoricals(raw, miss$variable)

4. Pass/Fail Target (cutoff = 61) + Factor Setup

Ordinal predictors get explicit level ordering (Low → High) so effects read monotonically; the rest become plain factors.

df <- add_target_and_factors(df)
table_class_balance(df)
Class Balance (cutoff = 61)
Status n pct
Pass 6462 97.8%
Fail 145 2.2%
 
plot_target_balance(df)

5. Univariate Distributions

num_vars <- c("Hours_Studied","Attendance","Sleep_Hours","Previous_Scores",
              "Tutoring_Sessions","Physical_Activity")
plot_num_distributions(df, num_vars)

8. Logistic Regression

Model P(Fail); positive coefficients raise failure risk. Exam_Score is excluded (it defines the target). Ordinal factors use polynomial contrasts, so .L (linear) terms capture the Low→High trend.

summary(fit)

9. Takeaways

  • Class balance: 2.2% fail (failing is the majority class here).
  • Strongest numeric signal: Attendance.
  • Strongest categorical signal: Learning_Disabilities.
  • One impossible score (101) was capped at 100.
  • Missingness was light (three categoricals, ~1%) and mode-imputed.
  • Exam_Score must stay out of any predictive model.
  • Because attendance and study hours dominate, an intervention model should probably weight those over the socioeconomic factors.
